lead.headline: Kenyan cult leader convicted over starvation deaths of 190 children
lead.dek: A Mombasa court found preacher Paul Mackenzie and 28 others guilty of murder over the Shakahola Forest deaths, with sentencing set for 6 November.
body: A court in Mombasa on Monday convicted Kenyan preacher Paul Mackenzie and 28 others of murder over the deaths of 191 people, 190 of them children, in one of the worst cult-linked tragedies in recent memory. Judge Diana Kavedza Mochache found that Mackenzie's group ran an organised system of religious radicalisation and enforced fasting that led to the deaths, and she rejected the defence argument that the victims had fasted voluntarily.

Prosecutors said Mackenzie, who led the Good News International Church, told followers that starving themselves and their children would carry them to heaven before the world ended. They described the plan as staged in phases, starting with the children. The judge said some children were isolated and denied food while their parents looked on, and Mackenzie reportedly also banned schooling and hospital care for his followers.

The case dates to 2023, when a tip-off led police to arrest Mackenzie and to find bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola Forest, near Kenya's southeastern coast. Authorities have since recovered more than 400 bodies, many still unidentified; Associated Press reporting said only 26 of the children had been identified. Police had been monitoring Mackenzie since 2017, and his church was shut down in 2019, after which he moved to the forest with followers.

Relatives of victims welcomed the outcome. Francis Wanje, who lost eight family members, said he was happy and had not expected a guilty verdict after such a long case. Director of Public Prosecutions Renson Ingonga called the convictions a significant achievement given the number of counts, accused people and witnesses involved. Defence lawyer Lawrence Obonyo said his clients were surprised and disappointed and would appeal.

Monday's ruling covered 191 murder counts. Mackenzie still faces other charges, including terrorism-related counts that he denies, and has pleaded not guilty in a separate case over 52 deaths in Kwa Binzaro village. Other deaths linked to the forest are the subject of separate proceedings. Sentencing for all 29 convicted people is expected on 6 November, and the defence says it has been instructed to appeal, so the legal process is far from over.
lead.why: The verdict is a landmark for Kenya's courts and a test of how the country regulates fringe religious groups and the long gap between early police monitoring of Mackenzie from 2017 and his arrest in 2023.

more.headline: Saudi Arabia postpones 'Davos in the Desert' to 2027 amid Houthi attacks
more.dek: The Future Investment Initiative, due in Riyadh from 26 to 29 October, has been pushed back with no new date set.
body: Saudi Arabia has postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative, nicknamed "Davos in the Desert", to 2027, with a new date to be announced. The tenth edition had been scheduled to run in Riyadh from 26 to 29 October. The conference's chief executive said the decision came from a commitment to partners, members, speakers and delegates. Al Jazeera reported that Ruth Porat of Alphabet, David Solomon of Goldman Sachs and Laurence Fink of BlackRock had been among the expected speakers.

The move follows weeks of Houthi attacks on the kingdom. Al Jazeera put the toll at no fewer than 18 killed and hundreds injured, with military, energy and civilian sites hit, including Riyadh's international airport. Riyadh government agencies told staff to work from home, and the 99-storey Kingdom Centre, which houses the IMF's regional office, asked workers to stay away. A 20 October security brief from the Foundation for Defense of Democracies said the airport was restricting air traffic. Fighting in Yemen has displaced more than 233,000 people, according to Al Jazeera.
more.why: The cancellation of the Gulf's biggest investor gathering shows the Yemen conflict is now hurting Saudi Arabia's economic showcase, not only its security.

lead.headline: Drone strike on Abyei market kills at least 153 people
lead.dek: The toll from Monday's attack in the disputed Sudan-South Sudan border zone more than doubled as fires slowed recovery of bodies.
body: A drone strike on a market in Abyei, a disputed and oil-rich area on the border between Sudan and South Sudan, has killed at least 153 people, according to the region's caretaker information minister, Yohana Akol Ngor. The strike hit around midday on Monday. Ngor said the toll had risen from an initial 73 and could climb further because fires were hampering the recovery of bodies. About 8,000 people have been displaced, and Médecins Sans Frontières said it was treating more than 20 wounded, some with burns, at Ameth Bek Hospital.

Responsibility is contested. South Sudanese officials, including Ngor, blamed Sudan's army but offered no evidence, and the army did not immediately respond. Reuters, citing three diplomatic sources, an aid worker and a conflict expert, reported that the strike hit a fuel depot the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) had used to supply their fighters. Sudan's military-led government says the RSF is active in parts of Abyei, which Ngor denies. Reuters could not verify either account, and the RSF did not respond to requests for comment. South Sudan's foreign ministry summoned the Sudanese ambassador in protest, while saying South Sudan has not taken sides in the war.

Both countries claim Abyei, which borders Sudan's Kordofan region, a major centre of fighting. The UN peacekeeping force there, UNISFA, warned in May that the RSF's presence had worsened insecurity. Sudan's war between the army and the RSF began in April 2023 and has produced one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

Drone strikes have escalated recently. Attacks hit Nyala and Khartoum airport this week, and a group called Emergency Lawyers attributed dozens of deaths in al-Muglad on 17 and 18 October to the army. A 10 October air strike near Sudan's border with Egypt killed more than 70 artisanal miners, according to a local rights group, and Chad has accused Sudan's military of drone strikes on its territory. An earlier tally of 73 dead in Abyei was reported in a 20 October security brief from the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. Democracy Now separately reported that a drone strike near a market in West Kordofan, in an area the RSF controls, killed 80 people on Sunday, one of the deadliest single strikes since the war began. The RSF blamed the army. More than 13 million people have been displaced by the war and 33.7 million need aid, according to that report.
lead.why: The strike widens Sudan's war toward a fragile border zone claimed by two states and raises the risk of a wider regional confrontation.

more.headline: Alberta voters reject a path toward independence from Canada
more.dek: Roughly three in four voters backed staying in Canada, a boost for Prime Minister Mark Carney, though separatists say the movement will continue.
body: Voters in the Canadian province of Alberta overwhelmingly rejected a move toward independence in a referendum. With more than 1.8 million votes counted, unofficial Elections Alberta figures reported by ITV showed about 75 percent in favour of remaining in Canada, while Al Jazeera's count put the figure near 76 percent. The ballot was not a direct vote on independence: it asked whether to hold another referendum on the subject, and a yes would have started a path toward a future separation vote.

Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed what he called a clear choice for unity. He said the roughly quarter of voters who backed the proposal should not automatically be counted as independence supporters, because some used the vote to express frustration with Ottawa, and he called for both sides to work together. Premier Danielle Smith, a conservative who called the referendum, said she voted against independence and that Albertans had chosen a stronger Alberta in a united Canada.

Separatists said the result would not end their campaign. Jeffrey Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project said the push would absolutely continue and ITV reported he wants Smith removed as leader of her United Conservative Party. Smith has said a federalist win should close the secession question. The vote drew outside interest, with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling Alberta a natural partner for Washington, according to Al Jazeera, while Carney is pursuing a new pipeline to export more Alberta bitumen overseas.
more.why: The result removes, for now, a major threat to Canadian unity, but the quarter of voters who wanted change signals lasting grievances in the oil-producing west.

more.headline: Japan launches probe to bring back samples from Mars's moon Phobos
more.dek: The MMX spacecraft lifted off on an H3 rocket and reached its planned orbit, starting a mission meant to return samples in 2031.
body: Japan launched its Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe on an H3 rocket from the Tanegashima Space Center at 4:41 a.m. on Tuesday, 20 October, Japan time (9:41 p.m. in Central Europe on Monday). About 1 hour 11 minutes after liftoff the spacecraft reached its planned orbit, and mission leader Yasuhiro Kawakatsu said it was in a stable condition, according to Nippon.com.

The plan is to travel to Mars, land on Phobos, the larger of the planet's two moons, collect surface samples and bring them back to Earth in 2031. If it succeeds, MMX will be the first mission to return samples from a Martian moon and the first round trip to the Martian system. The European Space Agency says MMX will be the first spacecraft to orbit Phobos and expects the probe to reach Mars next summer.

JAXA leads the mission, with partners including NASA, France's CNES, Germany's DLR and ESA. ESA supplied the spacecraft's deep-space communications equipment and ground-station support through its Estrack network, and European scientists sit on the science team. H3 project manager Makoto Arita said the launch opened the first chapter of the mission, and Nippon.com noted the H3 had now flown three consecutive successful launches.
more.why: Samples from Phobos could help settle whether the moons are captured asteroids or debris from a giant impact on Mars, and test the technology needed for future sample returns.

lead.headline: Oslo talks on Ukraine end without a deal as Witkoff heads to Putin
lead.dek: Zelenskyy met US envoy Steve Witkoff and European leaders in Norway, with Washington calling the talks constructive but no agreement reached.
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held talks in Oslo on Tuesday with US special envoy Steve Witkoff and European leaders, aiming to move the war with Russia toward negotiations. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said Zelenskyy had asked Witkoff and Jared Kushner to take part, and Kushner joined remotely because of illness. Finland was represented at leader level, and European and NATO officials also attended.

A US official described the talks as constructive and said they made "meaningful progress" toward a coordinated approach to dealing with Russia. Topics included security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic plan and Europe's wider security architecture. Witkoff wants to open a path to direct trilateral and multilateral negotiations and is due to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg. Finland's president said the peace process was back on track. No agreement was reached, and neither a Witkoff-Putin date nor a three-way leaders' meeting has been set.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv have worsened. President Donald Trump has publicly criticised Zelenskyy, accused him of not wanting to end the war and suggested someone else should negotiate for Ukraine. Kyiv says the United States has withheld military support and intelligence, which Washington denies. A source said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had not approved Ukraine's latest Patriot interceptor requests, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any deliberate policy change. Zelenskyy said he discussed guarantees modelled on NATO's Article 5 and Patriot supplies with Rubio, and that Ukraine is again receiving early warnings of Russian missile attacks.

A separate dispute concerns Starlink: Ukraine's access was disrupted, Hegseth said it had not been pulled back, and the Wall Street Journal reported Elon Musk ordered the slowdown after consulting Trump and administration officials. Zelenskyy has also called the US waiver of sanctions on Russian diesel exports a reward for Putin.

The fighting continued. A Russian drone hit the highway linking Kyiv and Odesa, killing three people and injuring four, and Russian strikes on three energy facilities of the company DTEK in the Odesa region left more than 32,000 families without power. In Russia's Tambov region, a Ukrainian drone attack started a fire at an oil pumping station, according to the governor.
lead.why: With US support in question and Russian strikes on Ukraine's grid intensifying, the talks decide whether Europe can hold a coordinated line before winter.

more.headline: Meta posts record revenue, but a legal charge and AI spending cut profit
more.dek: Third-quarter revenue rose 26 percent to $64.6 billion while free cash flow turned negative and the company announced a new class of non-voting shares.
body: Meta Platforms reported third-quarter revenue of $64.60 billion, up 26 percent from a year earlier and above analysts' expectation of about $63.3 billion. Net income was $9.86 billion, or $3.83 a share, after a $9.89 billion legal charge tied to a settlement with 52 state attorneys general; excluding that charge, earnings would have been $7.40 a share. Operating margin fell to 20 percent from 40 percent as costs rose 68 percent.

Spending on artificial intelligence was the other drag. Capital expenditure reached $34.91 billion, up about 80 percent, and exceeded operating cash flow of $32.79 billion, leaving free cash flow at negative $2.12 billion. Meta narrowed its 2026 capex forecast to $135 billion to $145 billion and guided fourth-quarter revenue to $73 billion to $76 billion. It said daily active people averaged 3.64 billion in September, and that more than 10 million people in the United States and Canada set up accounts for its Muse personal agent in about six weeks.

Meta will also issue non-voting Class C shares as a dividend, one for each Class A or B share, which works like a two-for-one split. The change takes effect once an amended certificate of incorporation becomes effective on 19 January 2027. SiliconANGLE reported that Mark Zuckerberg keeps about 60.6 percent of the vote on a 13.4 percent economic stake. Shares rose in after-hours trading, according to XTB, and SiliconANGLE reported they fell almost 8 percent the following day as investors weighed the AI spending.
more.why: Meta's results show how much of big tech's profit is being reinvested in AI infrastructure, and the new share class lets it raise money without diluting Zuckerberg's control.

more.headline: Tesla beats profit forecast as deliveries top estimates but margins stay thin
more.dek: Revenue was flat at $28.05 billion, and AI and robotics spending pushed operating income down 56 percent.
body: Tesla reported third-quarter revenue of $28.05 billion, flat on the year and in line with expectations, according to Electrek's account of the results. Adjusted earnings were 48 cents a share, ahead of the 45 cents analysts expected but 4 percent lower than a year earlier. GAAP net income fell 43 percent to $787 million, and operating income dropped 56 percent to $718 million because operating expenses rose 39 percent, with research and development up 69 percent on AI and Optimus robot spending.

Deliveries were 486,532 vehicles, down 2.1 percent from a year earlier but above the roughly 462,000 analysts expected, Tesla said in a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Production was 464,391 vehicles and the company deployed 13.7 gigawatt-hours of energy storage. Total gross margin improved to 19.6 percent from 18.0 percent a year earlier. Free cash flow was $1.53 billion, down from $3.99 billion.

Tesla said flat auto volumes reflected battery supply constraints and reported its largest passenger-vehicle order backlog in four years. Electrek reported that unsupervised full self-driving slipped to the second quarter of 2027 and will be limited to robotaxi zones, and that the company's robotaxi service had logged nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles.
more.why: Margins improved but profit fell as Tesla pours money into AI and robots, and the slip in unsupervised driving pushes back one of its most heavily promised products.

sources.name: Tesla filing, US Securities and Exchange Commission

lead.headline: Iran says seven ships hit in Hormuz as US and Europe weigh next move
lead.dek: The Revolutionary Guard's claim of its highest single-day toll in the strait is disputed by the US, while ministers urge diplomacy and Washington hints at strikes.
body: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Thursday that seven oil tankers were struck and damaged in the Strait of Hormuz, the highest single-day toll for the waterway since the United States and Israel began their war on Iran on 28 February. The Guards said four tankers were hit while transferring oil and caught fire overnight, and three were disabled after hitting mines. Al Jazeera said the claims could not be independently verified and gave no details on casualties or the ships' flags.

The Guards warned that if the trend continued, the conflict would extend to US bases in the region. President Donald Trump said Iran was inventing hits and mines to push up oil prices before the US midterm elections, and argued more oil was moving through Hormuz than before the war. An anonymous US Central Command spokesperson called the mine claims incorrect, said US forces had cleared the shipping lanes and that 95 percent of vessels were getting through, and described Iran's attacks as a sign of desperation under the American naval blockade. Before the war about one-fifth of the world's oil passed through the strait.

Iranian officials had signalled escalation. A 20 October security brief cited the Washington Post as reporting that Tehran planned to step up Hormuz attacks, expecting Trump to be less sensitive to energy prices after the midterms. Al Jazeera's reporting from Tehran said Iranian officials expect a US attack before the early-November vote, while its White House reporting said polls show most Americans want relief from war costs and rising fuel prices.

On Friday, foreign ministers from Britain, France, Germany, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Egypt and Italy met in Istanbul and urged the United States and Iran to pursue diplomacy rather than new strikes and to fully reopen the strait. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said none of the participants backed another attack on Iran, and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot warned that escalation would create only losers. US Ambassador to Türkiye Tom Barrack said Washington could strike Iran that weekend, but added that Trump wants a deal and that any action would not aim at regime change.
Oil markets are already tense. Al Jazeera reported Brent crude rose more than $2 to $110.85 a barrel on Wednesday, near a five-month high.
lead.why: A new round of US strikes would risk closing a route that carries a fifth of the world's oil at a time when emergency stockpiles are already low.

more.headline: US measles cases pass 4,500 as the country's 2026 total doubles last year's
more.dek: CDC data show 4,588 confirmed cases, though growth slowed to 4 percent for the week.
body: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention counted 4,588 confirmed measles cases in 2026 as of 22 October, up 178, or 4.0 percent, from 4,410 a week earlier, according to Contagion Live. The weekly rise was slower than the previous week's 8.1 percent, but the year's total is roughly double the 2,289 cases recorded in all of 2025. Cases span 47 jurisdictions, and 43 outbreaks have started this year. About 96 percent of cases are linked to outbreaks.

Hospitalizations reached 479, about 10 percent of cases, and 58 percent of patients are under 20. Some 96 percent of 2026 cases were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status. The CDC lists three measles deaths this year, a figure that may change as reviews finish, while a Pennsylvania coroner's report on 13 October described a sixth measles-related death in that state. Reuters reported on 16 October that Pennsylvania had 1,260 cases and 238 hospitalizations, that New York had declared a disaster emergency over the outbreak, and that the CDC had begun using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data to count measles deaths.

Kindergarten coverage with the MMR vaccine has fallen from 95.2 percent in 2019-20 to 92.4 percent in 2025-26, leaving about 280,000 kindergartners at risk, according to Contagion Live. The CDC counts only confirmed cases reported by states, so the true total may be higher.
more.why: Falling vaccination rates are allowing measles to spread again and CDC data show the outbreak is still growing, even if more slowly.

lead.headline: Israel locks down Hebron after attack kills two soldiers days before election
lead.dek: Netanyahu ordered the West Bank city sealed and prepared wider closures as the army launched a multi-day operation and arrests mounted.
body: Two Israeli soldiers were killed in a shooting attack at a checkpoint in northern Hebron, in the occupied West Bank, Al Jazeera reported on Friday, prompting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to order the city closed and to prepare a lockdown of the wider territory. The attack targeted a reserve battalion near the settlement of Telem. The military said it killed the two Palestinian gunmen, and two Palestinians were detained afterwards. Israel's ambulance service first reported at least five soldiers injured, two of whom later died. Witnesses said the shooting lasted about 20 minutes, which complicated evacuations.

Netanyahu called the response a reaction to a prevented "major attack" and cancelled election events, with Israel voting on Tuesday 27 October. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called for full Israeli control of the West Bank and for the Palestinian Authority to be dismantled and demilitarised. Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad and the PFLP praised the attack and called for more confrontations. The attack came as Israel prepared for its first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks; Democracy Now reported earlier in the week that President Trump had endorsed Netanyahu and that most polls showed his coalition short of a majority.

By Saturday, the Times of Israel reported, the army had launched a major operation in Hebron expected to last several days. Defence Minister Israel Katz said about 2,000 Palestinians had been displaced, Palestinians reported widespread closures and blocked roads, and the army had begun demolishing structures near the attack site.

Violence elsewhere in the territory also drew attention. On Thursday Israeli forces arrested 36 Palestinians across the West Bank, according to Wafa citing the Palestinian Prisoner's Society. The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission documented 17 attacks by soldiers and settlers on farmers during the olive harvest that day, including assaults, burned trees and live fire. US congressional candidate Brad Lander was briefly detained by the Israeli military on Wednesday while volunteering in the harvest.

The week began with settler attacks on harvesters. Democracy Now reported that about 80 masked settlers attacked Palestinians in Abu Falah, seriously injuring Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, whom they stabbed and robbed. US Ambassador Mike Huckabee called the attack terror, Netanyahu called reports of settler violence a smear campaign, and Israeli police detained 10 suspects.
lead.why: The crackdown lands days before an election in which security is a central issue, and it risks deepening a West Bank already strained by settler violence.

more.headline: Louvre, Orsay and Grand Palais shut as Paris braces for protests
more.dek: France's culture ministry closed leading museums on Saturday, and Art Basel Paris cancelled its weekend programme after opening to the public on Friday.
body: The Louvre, the Musée d'Orsay, the Picasso Museum and the Grand Palais were all closed on Saturday 24 October, according to a Culture Ministry statement to the Associated Press. The ministry told institutions under its authority to take the steps needed for visitor safety, staff protection and the preservation of artworks, after the previous weekend's protests turned violent with fires, looting and clashes with police. Al Jazeera said the Louis Vuitton Foundation also closed.

Art Basel Paris, which opened to the public only on Friday at the Grand Palais, cancelled its weekend programme, affecting 211 galleries, ABC News reported. About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed nationwide for the demonstrations over the cost of living, with helicopters, armoured vehicles and water cannon, and some marches were banned in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned that police would be uncompromising with anyone involved in violence. Rights groups criticised the restrictions: Amnesty International described them as a slide toward authoritarian practice, according to Al Jazeera.
more.why: Closing the world's most-visited museum shows how far the unrest has spread into daily life and into France's cultural calendar.

more.headline: Climate plans from 132 countries fall short on protecting health, new scorecard finds
more.dek: The Global Climate and Health Alliance ranks Colombia first and finds India, Japan and New Zealand at the bottom.
body: A new scorecard from the Global Climate and Health Alliance, a coalition of NGOs, assessed how well 132 countries' national climate plans protect health. Each plan was scored across eight indicators, including air pollution, healthcare-sector action, a just transition and financing, for a maximum of 32 points. Colombia topped the ranking with 29 points, followed by Nigeria with 25 and Cambodia with 24. The European Union ranked 12th, and 19 of the top 20 scorers were low- or middle-income economies.

Down To Earth reported that India scored 2 out of 32, joint bottom with Japan and New Zealand, because its plan does not mention air pollution. Only five countries, Cambodia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica and Paraguay, set black carbon reduction targets. The EU was the only major emitter with a specific air pollution target, a phase-out of hydrofluorocarbons by 2050. The United States scored 7 because its plan was not considered active after its withdrawal from the Paris Agreement.

Euronews reported that health ministries were closely involved in drawing up national climate plans in only 15 percent of the countries analysed. The alliance said governments cannot claim to put health first without tackling fossil fuel dependence, and it pointed to COP31 in November as a chance to turn the findings into more ambitious policy.
more.why: Air pollution and heat already cost lives, so climate plans that ignore health leave governments with weaker arguments and fewer allies for tougher action.

lead.headline: Hundreds of thousands march across France as nearly 1,000 are arrested
lead.dek: A week after rioting and looting, Saturday's protests over living costs passed with clashes in several cities under a 70,000-strong police deployment.
body: Hundreds of thousands of people took part in protests across France on Saturday over living costs, public services and school conditions. The interior ministry estimated 410,000 marchers nationwide, including 110,000 in Paris, while the CGT union said the figures were nearly double. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said police arrested nearly 1,000 people nationwide, including 64 in connection with the Paris demonstration, six of them minors.

Most marches were calm in the early hours, but clashes broke out later. In Paris police used tear gas and water cannon at the end of the march, and authorities said about 500 "rioters" clashed with officers, a lower level of violence than the previous weekend. Tear gas was also fired in Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, Grenoble, Lille and Nice, there were clashes in Marseille, and police in Dijon were targeted with fireworks. More than 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed, about 20 percent more than a week earlier, and at least 24 metro stations were closed. The Louvre and Musée d'Orsay shut for the day.

Saturday followed a far more violent weekend. More than half a million people marched on 17 October, over 2,000 people were taken into custody, and Fox News reported about 3,000 shops were damaged or looted. Nuñez had offered to resign, according to Democracy Now, but President Emmanuel Macron declined and blamed seditious ultra-left groups and criminals. Macron then said only union demonstrations would be authorised for the weekend, and local authorities banned marches in Lyon, Nice, Montpellier and Rouen.

Rights groups objected. Amnesty International described the restrictions as a slide toward authoritarian practice, and Human Rights Watch voiced alarm at reports of children severely injured by crowd-control weapons. Macron met high school student representatives on Friday and promised more teachers and an overhaul of the Parcoursup university admissions system, but students said it did not defuse tensions.

The movement has called another protest for next Saturday. Al Jazeera reported that Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella were expected to launch their presidential campaign on Sunday with a speech to about 10,000 supporters, and that a counter-protest of 20,000 to 30,000 people was expected in Orléans against the National Rally's congress.
lead.why: The unrest is testing Macron's government at the moment the far right begins its presidential campaign.

more.headline: Brewers edge Rays 3-2 in World Series opener after overturned double play
more.dek: Milwaukee led from the first inning, and a replay reversal let Tampa Bay score in the ninth before the Brewers closed it out.
body: The Milwaukee Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday 23 October at American Family Field to take a 1-0 lead. Christian Yelich hit an RBI triple in the first inning, in his first World Series game, and William Contreras drove in the second run with a single. Jackson Chourio drove in a run in the seventh to make it 3-1.

Brewers starter Jacob Misiorowski threw five innings, allowing one run on four hits with three strikeouts, and CBS Sports reported his first pitch of 103.5 mph was the fastest in World Series history in the pitch-tracking era. Tampa Bay's starter Nick Martinez also worked five innings with five strikeouts. The Rays' lower order went 1 for 17 with six strikeouts, and Jonathan Aranda was 3 for 3 and scored their first run.

The ninth inning was chaotic. Closer Trevor Megill loaded the bases with one out, and Liam Hicks appeared to ground into a game-ending double play, but replay overturned the call at second base, with CBS Sports noting the fielder did not hold the bag. A run scored to make it 3-2, and Megill then struck out Jonny DeLuca to end it. Game 2 was set for Saturday night in Milwaukee.
more.why: Winning the opener gives Milwaukee early control of a series in which Tampa Bay went hitless with runners in scoring position.

more.headline: World may have only a month or two of usable oil reserves, analysts warn
more.dek: With Brent near $111 and the US reserve at its lowest since 1982, a renewed Hormuz closure would hit stockpiles already drawn down.
body: Brent crude rose more than $2 to $110.85 a barrel on Wednesday, near a five-month peak, as fears grew of a renewed US-Iran war. Before the conflict began, about 20 million barrels a day, roughly a fifth of global supply, passed through the Strait of Hormuz. Al Jazeera reported that Kpler estimates a full Hormuz closure combined with a blocked Bab al-Mandeb could cut Middle Eastern crude exports from 16.8 million to 7.5 million barrels a day.

Emergency stocks are thin. The International Energy Agency's 32 members agreed on 11 March to release 400 million barrels, with the United States pledging 172.2 million and Japan 79.8 million. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve has fallen to 283 million barrels, its lowest since October 1982, and much of the oil was lent and must be returned with extra barrels. Global strategic stocks outside China and Iran have fallen nearly 327 million barrels since the end of December 2025, and analyst Aaron Kildow estimates only about 400 million barrels of usable reserves remain, nearly half of them in Japan.

IG Group's Chris Beauchamp said the world may have only a month or two of reserves if Hormuz shuts again, and called $150 a barrel a very real possibility. The IEA says diesel is already nearly double the price of crude. China holds 1.13 billion barrels in onshore stocks, about 80 days of refinery intake, while India's reserves cover about eight days of imports. Separately, the IEA has warned that Europe faces a difficult winter with low gas reserves, Al Jazeera reported.
more.why: Thin reserves leave importers, especially in Asia and Europe, with little cushion if the Gulf's main export route closes again.

lead.headline: Brazil votes in knife-edge runoff between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro
lead.dek: Final polls show a near dead heat as nearly 160 million eligible voters choose between the veteran president and the son of the jailed ex-president.
body: Brazilians went to the polls on Sunday to choose between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term for the Workers' Party, and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, of the Liberal Party. Polls opened at 8 a.m. local time (11:00 GMT) and close at 5 p.m. (20:00 GMT), with nearly 160 million people eligible to vote. No result was available when this edition was compiled.

The first round on 4 October was close: Bolsonaro took 47.03 percent of valid votes to Lula's 45.16 percent, according to the Rio Times, and neither passed 50 percent. Final polls showed a virtual tie. Futura had Bolsonaro at 50.1 percent and Lula at 49.9, while Datafolha and Quaest each had Bolsonaro at 51 and Lula at 49, and Palver had it 50 to 49. Al Jazeera noted that an AtlasIntel survey earlier in the campaign gave Bolsonaro 49.8 percent to Lula's 47.6, and that Lula had narrowed the gap since.

Bolsonaro promises a militarised approach to crime, closer partnership with the Trump administration, a debt ceiling and tighter control of inflation and spending. He has said he would redemocratise Brazil by reforming the constitution and has pledged to fight for the release of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for a coup plot after losing the 2022 election. Lula points to falling unemployment and poverty and reduced Amazon deforestation, but rising household debt and a polarised political landscape have limited his reform agenda.

The campaign has been bitter. The candidates held their only debate on 18 October. Protesters rallied outside Meta's offices in São Paulo accusing the company of interfering in the election, and Brazil's Electoral Court gave Meta 24 hours to prove it treats both campaigns equally, Democracy Now reported. A corruption scandal involving banker Daniel Vorcaro has implicated figures across the political spectrum, including Jair Bolsonaro, according to Al Jazeera. Large pro-Lula rallies have been held, and there are concerns about US interference, Al Jazeera reported. Results are expected soon after polls close.
lead.why: The result will decide whether Latin America's largest country stays with a left-wing government or turns toward a Trump-aligned right, and could embolden or deflate similar movements across the region.

more.headline: Serbia votes in snap election as Vučić faces a student-led challenge
more.dek: The president turned prime-ministerial candidate leads some polls, but others put the student list ahead after two years of protests.
body: Serbia held a snap parliamentary election on Sunday, called by President Aleksandar Vučić in September. Vučić, who has led the country as prime minister and then president for more than a decade, resigned the presidency to run for prime minister at the head of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). He is challenged by the Student List, a movement of about 250 mostly unfamiliar candidates, among them professors, actors and farmers, led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanović.

The race is tight. An Ipsos poll published on Thursday gave the SNS 47 percent and the students 40 percent, though other polls put the students ahead, according to Al Jazeera. Polling stations were open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., with first results expected about two hours after closing.

The Student List grew out of nearly two years of protests over corruption, triggered by the collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad's railway station in 2024, which killed 16 people. About 150,000 supporters rallied in central Belgrade on 22 October. Jacobin reported the list is targeting undecided voters, past abstainers and the diaspora, and noted irregularities and sporadic violence against opponents. Rights groups say repression has worsened. Vučić and his party deny accusations of repression, corruption and spying on opponents, and he claims the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, which they deny.

Vučić is promising higher pensions and public-sector pay, healthcare investment and subsidies for young couples. He has balanced ties with China and Russia while keeping the door open to EU membership, though relations with Brussels have frayed over judicial reform and the rule of law.
more.why: A loss for Vučić would end more than a decade of dominant rule in a candidate EU member, while a win would test whether the student movement can sustain pressure.
